Existential Calculi of Relations with Transitive Closure: Complexity and Edge Saturations Thanks: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP21K13828.
Yoshiki Nakamura

Abstract
We study the decidability and complexity of equational theories of the existential calculus of relations with transitive closure (ECoR*) and its fragments, where ECoR* is the positive calculus of relations with transitive closure extended with complements of term variables and constants. We give characterizations of these equational theories by using edge saturations and we show that the equational theory is 1) coNP-complete for ECoR* without transitive closure; 2) in coNEXP for ECoR* without intersection and PSPACE-complete for two smaller fragments; 3) Π 1 0 \Pi_{1}^{0} -complete for ECoR*. The second result gives PSPACE-upper bounds for some extensions of Kleene algebra, including Kleene algebra with top w.r.t. binary relations.



I
Introduction

The calculus of relations
(CoR, for short)
[
1
]
is an algebraic system on binary relations.
As binary relations appear everywhere in computer science, CoR and relation algebras (including their transitive closure extensions) can be applied to various areas, such as databases and program development and verification.
However, the equational theory of CoR is
undecidable

[
2
]
.
The undecidability holds even over the signature
\{\cdot,\cup,\_^{-}\}

of composition (
\cdot
), union (
\cup
), and complement (
\_^{-}
)
[
3
, Thm. 1]
, moreover even when the number of term variables is one
[
4
]
.

One approach to avoid the undecidability of the equational theory of CoR is to consider its
positive
fragments, by excluding complements.
The terms of
the positive calculus of relations
(
PCoR
, for short)
[
5
,
6
]

is the set of terms over the signature
\{\cdot,\cup,\_^{\smile},\bot,\top,\mathsf{I},\cap\}

of composition (
\cdot
), union (
\cup
), converse (
\_^{\smile}
), the empty relation (
\bot
), the universal relation (
\top
), the identity relation (
\mathsf{I}
), and intersection (
\cap
).
The equational theory of
PCoR
is
decidable

[
5
]
.
This decidability result also holds when adding the reflexive transitive operator, thus arriving at Kleene allegory terms
[
7
,
8
,
9
]
.

Then, it is natural to ask about the decidability and complexity of
PCoR
when the complement operator is added in restricted ways (cf. e.g.,
antidomain

[
10
,
11
]
and
tests
in Kleene algebra with tests (KAT)
[
12
]
) to extend the expressive power of
PCoR
without drastically increasing the complexity.
In this paper, inspired by the negations of atomic programs in the context of propositional dynamic logic (PDL)
[
13
,
14
,
15
]
,
we consider
existential calculi of relations
—positive calculi of relations extended with complements of term variables and constants (i.e., the complement operator only applies to term variables or constants)—and study the decidability and complexity of their equational theories.
We denote by
{\textrm{PCoR}}*
the
PCoR
with the reflexive transitive closure operator (
\_^{*}
).
We denote by
ECoR
(resp.
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
) the
PCoR
(resp.
{\textrm{PCoR}}*
) with complements of term variables and constants.
For example, whereas
(a\cdot a)^{-}
and
(a^{*})^{-}
are not
ECoR
terms,
ECoR
contains terms such as:

a^{-}

\left(\begin{array}[]{l}\mbox{there is \emph{not} an ($a$-labeled) edge}\\
\mbox{from the source to the target}\end{array}\right)

(a\cdot a)\cap a^{-}\cap\mathsf{I}^{-}

\left(\begin{array}[]{l}\mbox{the distance from the source}\\
\mbox{to the target is two}\end{array}\right)

They are not expressible in
PCoR
because they are not preserved under homomorphisms; thus,
ECoR
is strictly more expressive than
PCoR
.
More precisely, w.r.t. binary relations,
while
PCoR
has the same expressive power as the three-variable fragment of
existential positive
logic with equality
[
16
, Cor. 3.2]
,

ECoR
has the same expressive power as the three-variable fragment of
existential
logic with equality
[
16
, Cor. 3.14]
1
1

1

ECoR
has the same expressive power as the level
\Sigma_{1}^{\mathrm{CoR}}
of the
dot-dagger alternation hierarchy

[
17
]
[
16
, Def. 3.13]
of
\mathrm{CoR}
, because every
ECoR
term is a
\Sigma_{1}^{\mathrm{CoR}}
term,
and conversely, every
\Sigma_{1}^{\mathrm{CoR}}
term has an equivalent
ECoR
term by pushing complement and projection deeper into the term to the extent possible.
Here,
\Sigma_{1}^{\mathrm{CoR}}
has the same expressive power as the three-variable fragment of existential logic (i.e., the level
\Sigma_{1}
of the quantifier alternation hierarchy of first-order logic)
[
16
, Cor. 3.14]
.
.
(The name “
existential
calculi of relations” comes from this fact.)

On the equational theory of
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
, while it subsumes that of
{\textrm{PCoR}}*
(including axioms of Kleene algebra and allegory
[
6
]
),
some non-trivial valid (in)equations are as follows (see
Appendix

A
for the proofs):

\displaystyle\top

\displaystyle=a\cup a^{-}

(1)

\displaystyle aba^{-}

\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{I}^{-}a^{-}\cup a\mathsf{I}^{-}

(2)

\displaystyle a

\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{I}^{-}\cup aa

\displaystyle a^{\smile}a^{-}

To show them, we give a
graph theoretical characterization
of the equational theory of
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
(
Section

IV
).
The characterization using graph languages and graph homomorphisms is based on that for
{\textrm{PCoR}}*
, by Brunet and Pous
[
8
, Thm. 3.9]
[
6
, Thm. 16]
,
but the identical characterization fails for
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
.
Nevertheless, we can extend such a characterization even for
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
, by extending their graph languages, using
edge saturations
(cf. saturations of graphs
[
26
,
27
]
; in our saturation, the vertex set is fixed).
Using this graph characterization, we can show the upper bounds of
1)
and
3)
.

For the upper bound of
2)
: the equational theory of
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
without intersection,
we refine the graph characterization above by using path graphs with some additional information, called
saturable paths
(
Section

V
).
This notion is inspired by Hintikka-trees for Boolean modal logics
[
13
]
and PDL with the negation of atomic programs
[
14
]
,
where we consider paths instead of infinite trees and introduce the converse and the difference relation
\mathsf{I}^{-}
.
This characterization gives the coNEXP upper bound for the equational theory of
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
without intersection.
Moreover, for some fragments, we can give
word automata
using saturable paths, which shows that
the equational theory of
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
without intersection is decidable in PSPACE if
\mathsf{I}^{-}
does not occur (
Theorem

41
)
or if
a^{-}
does not occur (for any term variable
a
) (
Theorem

44
).
(Our automata construction cannot apply to the full case (
Remark

45
).)

For the lower bounds,
1)
and
2)
are immediate from the results known in regular expressions
[
18
,
19
]
.
For
3)
, we give a reduction from the universality problem for context-free grammars (
Section

VI
), via KA with hypotheses
[
28
,
29
,
30
]
of the form
t\leq a
(where
t
is a term and
a
is a term variable) w.r.t. binary relations.

briefly gives basic definitions.

Section

defines

(

) and recalls known results w.r.t. word and graph languages for smaller fragments of

,

).
In

, we give a graph theoretical characterization for

.

.

2)
.
In

, we prove the lower bound of
3)
.

Section

VII
concludes this paper.

II
Preliminaries

We write
\mathbb{N}
for the set of all non-negative integers.
For
l,r\in\mathbb{N}
, we write
[l,r]
for the set
\{i\in\mathbb{N}\mid l\leq i\leq r\}
.
For
n\in\mathbb{N}
, we write
[n]
for
[1,n]
.
For a set
A
, we write
\#(A)
for the cardinality of
A
and
\wp(A)
for the power set of
A
.

II-A

Graphs

For
k\in\mathbb{N}
, a
k
-pointed graph

G
over a set
A
is a tuple
\langle|G|,\{a^{G}\}_{a\in A},\mathsf{1}^{G},\dots,k^{G}\rangle
, where

•

|G|
is a non-empty set of
vertices
;

•

a^{G}\subseteq|G|^{2}
is a binary relation for each
a\in A
(
\langle x,y\rangle\in a^{G}
denotes that there is an
a
-labeled edge
from
x
to
y
);

•

\mathsf{1}^{G},\dots,k^{G}\in|G|
are the vertices pointed by
\mathsf{1},\dots,k
.

We say that
2
-pointed graphs are
graphs
, here; we mainly use them.
For
2
-pointed graph
G
, we say that
\mathsf{1}^{G}
and
\mathsf{2}^{G}
are the
source
and
target
, respectively.

A
(graph) homomorphism
from a graph
G
to a graph
H
is a map
h
from
|G|
to
|H|
such that

•

\langle h(\mathsf{1}^{G}),h(\mathsf{2}^{G})\rangle=\langle\mathsf{1}^{H},\mathsf{2}^{H}\rangle
;

•

\langle h(x),h(y)\rangle\in a^{H}
for every
a\in A
and
\langle x,y\rangle\in a^{G}
.

In particular, we say that
h
is
isomorphism
if
h
is bijective and
\langle h(x),h(y)\rangle\not\in a^{H}
for every
a\in A
and
\langle x,y\rangle\not\in a^{G}
.
We write
h\colon G\longrightarrow H
if
h
is a homomorphism from
G
to
H

and write
G\longrightarrow H
if
h\colon G\longrightarrow H
for some
h
.
The relation
\longrightarrow
is a preorder.
We display graphs in a standard way,
where the node having an ingoing (resp. outgoing) unlabeled arrow denotes the source (resp. the target).
For example, the following are two connected graphs, and dotted arrows induce a homomorphism between them:

a
b
a
b
.

term
t
on a structure
\mathfrak{A}
is defined as follows (where
a\in\Sigma
):

\displaystyle\llbracket a\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}a^{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\llbracket a^{-}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}(a^{-})^{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\llbracket\bot\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\emptyset

\displaystyle\llbracket\top\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}|\mathfrak{A}|^{2}

\displaystyle\llbracket t\cup s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\cup\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\llbracket t\cap s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\cap\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\llbracket\mathsf{I}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\mathsf{I}^{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\llbracket\mathsf{I}^{-}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}(\mathsf{I}^{-})^{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\llbracket t\cdot s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\cdot\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\llbracket t^{*}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\llbracket t^{n}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\llbracket t^{\smile}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}^{\smile}.

We write
\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t=s
if
\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
for every structure
\mathfrak{A}
.
The
equational theory over
S
w.r.t. binary relations
is defined as the set of all pairs
t=s
of terms in
\mathcal{T}_{S}
s.t.
\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t=s
.

Notation 2
.

Based on
\llbracket\_\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
, we define the following notations:

\displaystyle{\mathfrak{A}}[x,y]\models t

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\iff$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 5.0pt}}\langle x,y\rangle\in\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\models t=s

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\iff$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 5.0pt}}(\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\models t)\leftrightarrow(\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\models s)

\displaystyle\mathfrak{A}\models t=s

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\iff$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 5.0pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}.

(Note that
\mathfrak{A}\models t=s\iff\forall x,y\in|\mathfrak{A}|.\ {\mathfrak{A}}[x,y]\models t=s
.)

III-B

KA terms w.r.t. binary relations and word languages

For a set
X
, we write
X^{*}
for the set of all finite sequences (i.e.,
words
) over
X
.
We write
\mathsf{I}
for the empty word.
We write
wv
for the concatenation of words
w
and
v
.
For set
L,K\subseteq\Sigma^{*}
, the
composition

L\cdot K
is defined by:

L\cdot K\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{wv\mid w\in L\ \land\ v\in K\}.

The
(word) language

[t]\subseteq\Sigma^{*}
of a KA term
t
is defined by:

\displaystyle[a]

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{a\}

\displaystyle[\bot]

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\emptyset

\displaystyle[t\cup s]

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}[t]\cup[s]

\displaystyle[\mathsf{I}]

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{\mathsf{I}\}

\displaystyle[t\cdot s]

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}[t]\cdot[s]

\displaystyle[t^{*}]

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}[t^{n}].

Interestingly, for KA terms, it is well-known that the equational theory w.r.t. binary relations coincides with that under the (single) word language interpretation (see, e.g.,
[
6
, Thm. 4]
):
for every KA terms
t,s
, we have

{}\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s\quad\iff\quad[t]\subseteq[s].

(
\dagger
)

The following follows from (

†

‣
III-B
) and the known results in regular expressions
[
18
, p. 3]
(
[
19
]
, for precise constructions):

Proposition 3

(
[
19
, Thm. 2.7]
,
[
18
]
)
.

The equational theory of
\mathcal{T}_{\{\cdot,\cup\}}
(w.r.t. binary relations) is coNP-complete.

Proposition 4

(
[
19
, Prop. 2.4]
,
[
18
]
)
.

The equational theory of
\mathcal{T}_{\{\cdot,\cup,\_^{*}\}}
(w.r.t. binary relations) is PSPACE-complete.

They can show the lower bounds of
Theorems

24
,
41
,
44
.

Remark 5
.

The equivalence (

†

‣
III-B
) breaks if we add
\cap
,
\_^{\smile}
, or
\top
by a standard word language interpretation
[
6
, Sect. 4]
.
Note that (

†

‣
III-B
) also breaks if we add
a^{-}
or
\mathsf{I}^{-}
with
[a^{-}]\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\Sigma^{*}\setminus\{a\}

and
[\mathsf{I}^{-}]\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\Sigma^{*}\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\}
, respectively.
For example,
\models_{\mathrm{REL}}\top a\top b\top=\top b\top a\top
holds
[
6
, p. 13]
, but their languages are not the same.
Here,
\top
abbreviates the term
c\cup\overline{c}
(cf.
Equation

1
) where
c
is any.
Conversely, for example,
[a^{-}]=[\mathsf{I}\cup(\Sigma\setminus\{a\})\cup(\Sigma\cdot\Sigma\cdot\Sigma^{*})]
holds,
but such an equation does not hold in relational semantics (where a finite set
L=\{t_{1},\dots,t_{n}\}
of terms abbreviates the term
t_{1}\cup\dots\cup t_{n}
, here).

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{G^{\smile}\mid G\in\mathcal{G}(t)\}.

Definition 7
.

For a graph
G
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
, the
binary relation

\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\subseteq|\mathfrak{A}|^{2}
on a structure
\mathfrak{A}
is defined by:

\langle x,y\rangle\in\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\quad\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\iff$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 5.0pt}}\quad(G\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x,y]).

(
G\longrightarrow H
denotes that there is a homomorphism from
G
to
H
.)
For each graph language
\mathcal{G}
, let

\llbracket\mathcal{G}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}.

Based on
\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
and
\llbracket\mathcal{G}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
, we use
\models
(
2
) also for graphs and graph languages.
Note that:

\displaystyle\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\models G

\displaystyle\iff G\longrightarrow\ddot{\mathfrak{A}};

\displaystyle\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\models\mathcal{G}

\displaystyle\iff\exists G\in\mathcal{G}.G\longrightarrow\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}.

The graph languages above characterize the relational semantics and the equational theory for
{\textrm{PCoR}}*
, as follows
(
Proposition

8
is shown by induction on
t
and
Proposition

9
is shown by using
Proposition

8
; see
Appendix

C
, for more details):

Proposition 8
.

For every structure
\mathfrak{A}
and PCoR* term
t
,

\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{G}(t)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}.

Proposition 9

(
[
8
, Thm. 3.9]
,
[
6
, Thm. 16]
)
.

For every
{\textrm{PCoR}}*
terms
t,s
, we have

{}\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s\iff\forall G\in\mathcal{G}(t).\exists H\in\mathcal{G}(s).\ H\longrightarrow G.

.

)
.

IV-A

Edge-saturated graphs and 2-pointed structures

For a binary relation
R
, we write
R^{\mathcal{E}}
for the
equivalence closure
of
R
(the minimal equivalence relation subsuming
R
).

For a graph
G
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
, we write
G^{\mathcal{Q}}
for the quotient graph
7
7

7

Precisely,
G^{\mathcal{Q}}
is the graph over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
, defined by

|G^{\mathcal{Q}}|=\{[x]_{G}\mid x\in G\}
;

a^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}}=\{\langle X,Y\rangle\in|G^{\mathcal{Q}}|^{2}\mid\exists x\in X.\ \exists y\in Y.\ \langle x,y\rangle\in a^{G}\}
for
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
;

\langle\mathsf{1}^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}},\mathsf{2}^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}}\rangle=\langle[\mathsf{1}^{G}]_{G},[\mathsf{2}^{G}]_{G}\rangle
.
of
G
w.r.t. the equivalence relation
(\mathsf{I}^{G})^{\mathcal{E}}
;

.
We use
[x]_{G}
to denote the quotient set of a vertex
x\in|G|
w.r.t. the equivalence relation
(\mathsf{I}^{G})^{\mathcal{E}}
.

Definition 13
.

Let
G
be a graph over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
.
We say that
G
is
consistent
if for every
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}
, the following holds:

(
a
-consistent)

((\mathsf{I}^{G})^{\mathcal{E}}\cdot a^{G}\cdot(\mathsf{I}^{G})^{\mathcal{E}})\cap((\mathsf{I}^{G})^{\mathcal{E}}\cdot\overline{a}^{G}\cdot(\mathsf{I}^{G})^{\mathcal{E}})=\emptyset
.

We say that
G
is
(consistently) edge-saturated
if
G
is consistent and the following hold:

(
a
-saturated)

a^{G}\cup\overline{a}^{G}=|G|^{2}
, for every
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}
;

(I-equivalence)

\mathsf{I}^{G}
is an equivalence relation.

Each edge-saturated graph induces a
2
-pointed structure:

Proposition 14
.

If a graph
G
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
is edge-saturated, then
G^{\mathcal{Q}}
is a
2
-pointed structure.

Proof.

\mathsf{I}^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}}
is the identity relation because
\mathsf{I}^{G}
is an equivalence relation
(I-equivalence)
.
For
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}
,
\bar{a}^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}}=|G^{\mathcal{Q}}|^{2}\setminus a^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}}
holds because

a^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}}\cup\bar{a}^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}}=|G^{\mathcal{Q}}|^{2}

(

a

-saturated)

and
a^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}}\cap\bar{a}^{G^{\mathcal{Q}}}=\emptyset

(

a

-consistent)
.
Thus,
G^{\mathcal{Q}}
is a
2
-pointed structure.
∎

IV-B

Graph characterization via edge saturations

Definition 15
.

For graphs
G,H
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
,
we say that
H
is an
edge-extension
of
G
, if
|H|=|G|
and
a^{H}\supseteq a^{G}
for every
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
.
We say that
H
is an
(edge-)saturation
of
G
if

H
is an edge-extension of
G
and is edge-saturated.

Let
\mathcal{S}(G)
be the set of all saturations of
G
.

For a graph language
\mathcal{G}
,
let
\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{G})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\mathcal{S}(G)
and
\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{G})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{G^{\mathcal{Q}}\mid G\in\mathcal{G}\}
.
We abbreviate
\mathcal{Q}\circ\mathcal{S}
to
\mathcal{QS}
.

As above, by using
\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(\top))
instead of
\mathcal{G}(\top)
, we can avoid the problem in
Example

12
.
Using
\mathcal{QS}
, we can strengthen
Proposition

9
(
[
8
, Thm. 3.9]
,
[
6
, Thm. 16]
), for
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
, as
Theorem

18
.
We first show the following:

Lemma 17
.

For any graph
G
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
,

\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{QS}(G)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.

Proof.

We prove that for any
G
, both
\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{S}(G)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
and
\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket G^{\mathcal{Q}}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
, respectively.

For
\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{S}(G)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
:
(
\supseteq
):
If
H\in\mathcal{S}(G)
and
h\colon H\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
,
then
h\colon G\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
because
H
is a saturation of
G
.
(
\subseteq
):
If
h\colon G\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
,
let
H
be the saturation of
G
s.t.
a^{H}=\{\langle x,y\rangle\mid\langle h(x),h(y)\rangle\in a^{\mathfrak{A}}\}
for
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
.
Then
h\colon H\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
.
Here,
H
is an edge-extension of
G
because
\langle x,y\rangle\in a^{G}\Longrightarrow\langle h(x),h(y)\rangle\in a^{\mathfrak{A}}\Longrightarrow\langle x,y\rangle\in a^{H}
;

H
is edge-saturated because
\mathfrak{A}
is edge-saturated; thus,
H
is indeed a saturation of
G
.
For example, from the homomorphism for
G\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
, by filling non-existing edges in
G
so that they map to edges of
{\mathfrak{A}}
,
we can construct the saturation
H
of
G
s.t.
H\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
, as follows:

\displaystyle G=\hskip-5.0pt\hbox to85.28pt{\vbox to15.45pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 14.18736pt\lower-12.11949pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

For
\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket G^{\mathcal{Q}}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
:
(
\supseteq
):
If
G^{\mathcal{Q}}\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
,
then
G\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
because
G\longrightarrow G^{\mathcal{Q}}
by the quotient map (with transitivity of
\longrightarrow
).
(
\subseteq
):
If
h\colon G\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
,
then
h\circ g\colon G^{\mathcal{Q}}\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x_{0},y_{0}]
, where
g
is a section of the quotient map from
G
to
G^{\mathcal{Q}}
(a map
g
s.t.
g(X)\in X
for
X\in|G^{\mathcal{Q}}|
).
Hence,
\llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{S}(G)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{QS}(G)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.
∎

Theorem 18

(cf.
Proposition

9
)
.

For every
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
terms
t,s
,

{}\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s\iff\forall G\in\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t)).\exists H\in\mathcal{G}(s).\ H\longrightarrow G.

Proof.

By the following formula transformation:

\displaystyle{}\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s\iff\forall\mathfrak{A}.\ \llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\subseteq\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

(Def. of
\models_{\mathrm{REL}}
)

\displaystyle\iff\forall\mathfrak{A}.\ \llbracket\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t))\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\subseteq\llbracket\mathcal{G}(s)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

(
Propositions

11
,
17
)

\displaystyle\iff\forall\mathfrak{A}.\forall G\in\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t)).\ \llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\subseteq\llbracket\mathcal{G}(s)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

(Def. of
\llbracket\rrbracket
)

\displaystyle\iff\forall G\in\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t)).\forall\mathfrak{A}.\ \llbracket G\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\subseteq\llbracket\mathcal{G}(s)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\iff\forall G\in\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t)).\forall\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}.

\displaystyle\quad(G\longrightarrow\ddot{\mathfrak{A}})\mbox{ implies }(\exists H\in\mathcal{G}(s).\ H\longrightarrow\ddot{\mathfrak{A}})

(Def. of
\llbracket\rrbracket
)

\displaystyle\iff\forall G\in\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t)).\exists H\in\mathcal{G}(s).\ H\longrightarrow G.

(
\heartsuit
)

Here, for (

♡

‣
IV-B
),

\Longleftarrow
:

H\in\mathcal{G}(s)
be such that
H\longrightarrow G

Then for any
2
-pointed structure
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}

\longrightarrow

\Longrightarrow
:

(
Proposition

14
).
∎

IV-C

Bounded model property

Theorem

18
gives an upper bound for the equational theories of existential calculi of relations.
Note that the model checking problem of
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
is decidable in polynomial time.

Proposition 20
.

The following problem is decidable in
\mathcal{O}(\|t\|\times\#(|\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}|)^{\omega})
time:
given a finite
2
-pointed structure
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}
and an
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
term
t
, does
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\models t
hold?
Here,
\omega
is the matrix multiplication exponent.

Proof Sketch.

Let
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}={\mathfrak{A}}[x,y]
.
For
s\in\mathrm{Sub}(t)
,
let
f_{s}\colon|\mathfrak{A}|\times|\mathfrak{A}|\to\{\mathsf{true},\mathsf{false}\}
be such that

f_{s}(x,y)=\mathsf{true}
iff
\langle x,y\rangle\in\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.
Here,
\mathrm{Sub}(t)
denotes the set of all sub-terms of
t
.
Then the function tables of
\{f_{s}\}_{s\in\mathrm{Sub}(t)}
can be calculated by a simple dynamic programming on
s
,
where for the case
s={u}^{*}
,
we use the algorithm for the transitive closure of boolean matrix
[
31
]
.
∎

Lemma 21

(bounded model property)
.

For every
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
terms
t
,
s
,
we have:

{}\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s

\iff

there exists a
2
-pointed structure
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\in\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t))
such that
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\not\models t\leq s
.

Proof.

\Longleftarrow
: Trivial.

\Longrightarrow
:
Let
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}={\mathfrak{A}}[x,y]\in\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t))
be a
2
-pointed structure such that
\forall H\in\mathcal{G}(s)
,
H\not\longrightarrow\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}
(
Theorem

18
).
Then
\langle x,y\rangle\in\llbracket\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t))\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
because
\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t))\ni\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\longrightarrow{\mathfrak{A}}[x,y]
(
\longrightarrow
is reflexive).

\langle x,y\rangle\not\in\llbracket\mathcal{G}(s)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
because
\forall H\in\mathcal{G}(s).\ H\not\longrightarrow\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}
(Def. of
\llbracket\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
).
Thus
\langle x,y\rangle\in\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
and
\langle x,y\rangle\not\in\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
(
Propositions

11
,
17
).
Hence
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\not\models t\leq s
.
∎

Lemma 22
.

The equational theory of
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
is in
\Pi_{1}^{0}
.

Proof.

Since
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t=s
if and only if
(\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s)\lor(\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}s\leq t)
,
it suffices to show that the following problem is in
\Sigma_{1}^{0}
:
given
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
terms
t,s
, does
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s
hold?
This follows from
Lemma

21
with
Proposition

20
.
Note that for every
G\in\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t))
,
\#(|G|)
is always finite,
and that we can easily enumerate the graphs in
\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t))
.
∎

Particularly for
ECoR
(not
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
), graphs of each term
t
have a linear number of vertices in the size
\|t\|
.

Proposition 23
.

For every
ECoR
term
t
and
G\in\mathcal{QS}(\mathcal{G}(t))
, we have
\#(|G|)\leq 1+\|t\|
.

Proof Sketch.

By easy induction on
t
, we have: for every
H\in\mathcal{G}(t)
,
\#(|H|)\leq 1+\|t\|
.
Also
\#(|G|)\leq\#(|H|)
is clear for every
G\in\mathcal{QS}(H)
.
∎

Theorem 24
.

The equational theory of
ECoR
is coNP-complete.

Proof.

For hardness: By
proposition

3
, as
ECoR
subsumes
\mathcal{T}_{\{\cdot,\cup\}}
.
For upper bound:
Similarly for
lemma

22
,
we show that the following problem is in NP: given
ECoR
terms
t,s
, does
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s
hold?
By
Lemma

21
, we can give the following algorithm:

1.

Take a graph
H\in\mathcal{G}(t)
non-deterministically according to the definition of
\mathcal{G}
;
then take a graph
G\in\mathcal{S}(H)
, non-deterministically (
G
is a graph in
\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{G}(t))
).

2.

Return
\mathsf{true}
if
G^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models t\leq s
;
\mathsf{false}
otherwise.

Then
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s
if some execution returns
\mathsf{true}
;
\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s
otherwise.
Here,
G^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models t\leq s
can be decided in polynomial time by

Proposition

20
with
\#(|G^{\mathcal{Q}}|)\leq 1+\|t\|
(
Proposition

23
).
∎

V
saturable paths: saturations from a path graph for intersection-free fragments

In this section, we refine the graph characterization of edge-saturations (in the previous section) for
{\textrm{ECoR}}*
without intersection (
ExKA
, for short;
Section

III-A
) by using
saturable paths
.
Using this characterization, we can show the decidability of the equational theory (
Theorem

33
) and give an automata construction for two smaller fragments (
Theorems

40
,
43
).

V-A

NFAs as terms

A
non-deterministic finite automaton with epsilon translations
\mathsf{I}
(NFA, for short)
\mathcal{A}=\langle|\mathcal{A}|,\{a^{\mathcal{A}}\}_{a\in A},\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}},\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\rangle
over a set
A
(with
A
containing a designated element
\mathsf{I}
) is a graph over
A
.
The
transition relation

\delta_{w}^{\mathcal{A}}
of a word
w=a_{1}\dots a_{n}\in(A\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\})^{*}
is defined by:

\delta_{w}^{\mathcal{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}(\mathsf{I}^{\mathcal{A}})^{*}\cdot a_{1}^{\mathcal{A}}\cdot(\mathsf{I}^{\mathcal{A}})^{*}\cdot\ldots\cdot(\mathsf{I}^{\mathcal{A}})^{*}\cdot a_{n}^{\mathcal{A}}\cdot(\mathsf{I}^{\mathcal{A}})^{*}.

For notational simplicity, for
x\in|\mathcal{A}|
and
X\subseteq|\mathcal{A}|
,
let
\delta_{w}^{\mathcal{A}}(x)\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{y\mid\langle x,y\rangle\in\delta_{w}^{\mathcal{A}}\}
and
\delta_{w}^{\mathcal{A}}(X)\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{x\in X}\delta_{w}^{\mathcal{A}}(x)
.
The
language

[\mathcal{A}]
of
\mathcal{A}
is defined by:

[\mathcal{A}]\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{w\in(A\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\})^{*}\mid\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\in\delta_{w}^{\mathcal{A}}(\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}})\}.

Let
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{a,a^{\smile}\mid a\in\Sigma^{(-)}\}\cup\{\mathsf{I},\mathsf{I}^{-}\}
.
Similarly for
\overline{t}
,
for each
t\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\cup\{\bot,\top\}
,

\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{189327}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle t\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{189327}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle t\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{158379}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle t\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{147761}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle t\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}
denotes the following term, where
a\in\Sigma^{(-)}
:

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{277133}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{277133}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{227418}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{203012}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}a^{\smile}

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{721325}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle a^{\smile}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{721325}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle a^{\smile}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{610446}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle a^{\smile}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{586040}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle a^{\smile}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}a

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{145637}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle\mathsf{I}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{145637}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle\mathsf{I}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{101945}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle\mathsf{I}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{72818}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{I}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\mathsf{I}

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{313119}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle\mathsf{I}^{-}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{313119}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle\mathsf{I}^{-}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{251952}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle\mathsf{I}^{-}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{222825}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{I}^{-}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\mathsf{I}^{-}

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{524288}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle\top\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{524288}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle\top\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{444188}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle\top\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{400499}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle\top\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\top

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{524288}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle\bot\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{524288}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle\bot\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{444188}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle\bot\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{400499}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle\bot\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bot.

In the following, we always consider NFAs over the set
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
(where
\mathsf{I}
is used as epsilon transitions).

For an NFA
\mathcal{A}
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
,
the
binary relation

\llbracket\mathcal{A}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\subseteq|\mathcal{A}|^{2}
is defined by:

\llbracket\mathcal{A}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{w\in[\mathcal{A}]}\llbracket w\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}.

Naturally, we can give a construction from
ExKA
terms to NFAs using Thompson’s construction
[
32
]
, as follows:

.

Proposition 26
.

For every structure
\mathfrak{A}
and
ExKA
term
t
, we have
\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{A}_{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.

Proof Sketch.

Let
s
be the term
t
in which each
\top
has been replaced with
a\cup\overline{a}
.
Then,
\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
holds by
Equation

1

and
\mathcal{A}_{s}
coincides with
\mathcal{A}_{t}
(by
Definition

25
).
By viewing
s
as the regular expression over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\}
, we have
[s]=[\mathcal{A}_{s}]

[
32
]
.
By straightforward induction on
s
using the distributivity,
\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\bigcup_{w\in[s]}\llbracket w\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
(
Appendix

E
).
Thus
\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\bigcup_{w\in[s]}\llbracket w\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\bigcup_{w\in[\mathcal{A}_{s}]}\llbracket w\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{A}_{s}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{A}_{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.
∎

Thanks to the above proposition, we work directly with NFAs rather than terms in the sequel.

V-B

Saturable paths

For a word
w\in(\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\})^{*}
,
we use
G(w)
to denote the unique graph in
\mathcal{G}(w)
(
Definition

6
), up to isomorphism.
Here, each vertex in
G(w)
is indexed by a number in
[0,n]
, from the left to the right,
where
w=a_{1}\dots a_{n}
.

(

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}.

Here the states under each vertex denote that they are reachable from the state
\mathtt{A}
on the vertex
0
;
more precisely, each set
U_{i}\subseteq|\mathcal{A}|
(where
i\in|G(w)|
) is defined by:

\displaystyle z\in U_{i}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\iff$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 5.0pt}}\exists v\in[{\mathcal{A}}[\_,z]].\ G(v)\longrightarrow H^{\mathcal{Q}}[\_,[i]_{H}].

Here,
{\mathcal{A}}[\_,z]
denotes the graph
\mathcal{A}
in which
\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}
has been replaced with
z
(similarly for
H^{\mathcal{Q}}[\_,[i]_{H}]
).
By definition,
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models\mathcal{A}
(iff
\lnot(\exists v\in[{\mathcal{A}}].\ G(v)\longrightarrow H^{\mathcal{Q}})
) iff
\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\not\in U_{\mathsf{2}^{H}}
.
For example, in
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}H_{2}}
,

Using only the data of
P
, we can show the existence of a saturation of
G(w)
.
For each pair
\langle i,j\rangle
of vertices,
if (
\delta_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i})\subseteq U_{j}
and
\delta_{\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{227418}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{227418}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{135795}{124882}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{96996}{89202}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{j})\subseteq U_{i}
) or
(
\delta_{\overline{a}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i})\subseteq U_{j}
and
\delta_{\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{262145}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle\overline{a}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{262145}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle\overline{a}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{262145}{124882}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle\overline{a}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{262145}{89202}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle\overline{a}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{j})\subseteq U_{i}
) holds (cf.
(P-Sat)
in

then we add either the

for example, for the pair

(See
Remark

45
for an example when there is no saturation.)

Inspired by
\{U_{i}\}_{i\in|G(w)|}
above, for characterizing the saturability problem, we define
saturable paths
;
they are path graphs with additional data (an equivalence relation
\mathsf{I}
, its complement
\overline{\mathsf{I}}
, and
\{U_{i}\}_{i\in|G(w)|}
) for taking saturations appropriately.
For graphs
G,H
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
,
we say that
H
is an
\mathsf{I}
-saturation
of
G
if

H
is an edge-extension of
G
such that

•

for every
a\in\Sigma^{(-)}
,
a^{H}=a^{G}
;

•

\mathsf{I}^{H}
is an equivalence relation and
\overline{\mathsf{I}}^{H}=|H|^{2}\setminus\mathsf{I}^{H}
;

•

H
is consistent.

(By definition,
H
is uniquely determined from
\mathsf{I}^{H}
, if exists.)

Definition 29

(saturable path)
.

For an NFA
\mathcal{A}
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
and a word
w
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\}
,
consider a pair
P=\langle G,\{U_{i}\}_{i\in|G|}\rangle
of

•

G
an
\mathsf{I}
-saturation of
G(w)
;

•

U_{i}\subseteq|\mathcal{A}|
for each
i\in|G|
.

For
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
, let

\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U,U^{\prime})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}(\delta_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U)\subseteq U^{\prime}\land\delta_{\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{227418}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{227418}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{135795}{124882}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{96996}{89202}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U^{\prime})\subseteq U).

Then we say that
P
is a
saturable path
for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
if the following three hold:

(P-s-t)

\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}}\in U_{\mathsf{1}^{G}}
and
\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\not\in U_{\mathsf{2}^{G}}
;

(P-Con)

for all
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
and
\langle i,j\rangle\in a^{G}
,
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
;

(P-Sat)

for all
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}
and
\langle i,j\rangle\in|G|^{2}
,

\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})\lor\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{a}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
.

Saturable paths can characterize the saturability problem, as
Lemma

32
.
We first show the following:

Lemma 30
.

For every saturable path
P=\langle G,\{U_{i}\}_{i\in|G|}\rangle
for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
,
there is a saturation
H
of
G
such that

(P-Con’)

for all
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-)}
and
\langle i,j\rangle\in a^{H}
,
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
.

Proof.

Starting from
H=G
, we add edges labeled with
a\in\Sigma^{(-)}
while preserving
(P-Con’)
, by repeating the following:

•

If
\langle i,j\rangle\in(\mathsf{I}^{H}\cdot a^{H}\cdot\mathsf{I}^{H})\setminus a^{H}
for some
a\in\Sigma^{(-)}
and
i,j\in|H|
,
we add the edge to
H
.
Then,
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
holds as follows.
Let
i^{\prime},j^{\prime}
be s.t.
\langle i,i^{\prime}\rangle\in\mathsf{I}^{H}
,
\langle i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\rangle\in a^{H}
, and
\langle j^{\prime},j\rangle\in\mathsf{I}^{H}
.
For every
z\in|\mathcal{A}|
,
we have

\displaystyle z\in U_{i^{\prime}}

\displaystyle\Longrightarrow z\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i})

(
U_{i^{\prime}}\subseteq\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i})

(P-Con’)
)

\displaystyle\Longrightarrow z\in U_{i}

(
\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}=(\mathsf{I}^{\mathcal{A}})^{*}
is reflexive)

\displaystyle\dots\Longrightarrow z\in U_{i^{\prime}}.

(
\mathsf{I}^{H}
is symmetric)

Thus
U_{i}=U_{i^{\prime}}
.
In the same way,
U_{j}=U_{j^{\prime}}
.
Hence
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
is derived from
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i^{\prime}},U_{j^{\prime}})
.

•

Otherwise, since
H
is not edge-saturated,
\langle i,j\rangle\not\in a^{H}\cup\overline{a}^{H}
for some
a\in\Sigma
and
i,j\in|H|
.
If
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
holds, then we add the edge for
\langle i,j\rangle\in a^{H}
to
H
.
Otherwise, since
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{a}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
holds by
(P-Sat)
,
we add the edge for
\langle i,j\rangle\in\overline{a}^{H}
to
H
.

Then
H
is a saturation of
G
, as follows.
For
(I-equivalence)
:
Because
G
is an
\mathsf{I}
-saturation.
For
(

a

-saturated)
: Clear.
For
(

a

-consistent)
:
By that
G
is consistent and
(\mathsf{I}^{H}\cdot a^{H}\cdot\mathsf{I}^{H})\cap(\mathsf{I}^{H}\cdot\overline{a}^{H}\cdot\mathsf{I}^{H})=\emptyset
is preserved (by the construction of
H
).
∎

First, we add the
a
-labeled edge for
\langle 2,1\rangle
because
\langle 2,1\rangle\in(\mathsf{I}^{G}\cdot a^{G}\cdot\mathsf{I}^{G})
; similarly, we add the
\overline{a}
-labeled edge for
\langle 1,0\rangle
(let
G^{\prime}
be the graph).
Second, we consider adding an
a
- or
\overline{a}
-labeled edge for
\langle 0,2\rangle
.
Then, because
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(\{\mathtt{A,C}\},\{\mathtt{A,C}\})
, we add an
a
-labeled edge for
\langle 0,2\rangle
(note that
\lnot\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{a}}^{\mathcal{A}}(\{\mathtt{A,C}\},\{\mathtt{A,C}\})
because
\delta_{\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{262145}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle\overline{a}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{262145}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle\overline{a}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{262145}{124882}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle\overline{a}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{262145}{89202}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle\overline{a}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}}^{\mathcal{A}}(\{\mathtt{A,C}\})=\{\mathtt{D}\}\not\subseteq\{\mathtt{A,C}\}
); we also add an
a
-labeled edge for
\langle 2,0\rangle
because
\langle 2,0\rangle,\langle 0,2\rangle\in\mathsf{I}^{G^{\prime}}
(let
G^{\prime\prime}
be the graph).
By adding the other edges similarly, the saturation
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
of
G(w)
can be obtained.

Lemma 32
.

For an NFA
\mathcal{A}
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
and a word
w
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\}
,
the following are equivalent:

•

There is a saturation
H
of
G(w)
such that
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models w\leq\mathcal{A}
.

•

There is a saturable path
P
for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
.

Proof.

\Longleftarrow
:
Let
P=\langle G,\{U_{i}\}_{i\in|G|}\rangle
.
Let
H
be the saturation of
G
(
Lemma

30
).
Then
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models w\leq\mathcal{A}
holds as follows.
For
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\models w
:
Because
G(w)\longrightarrow H\longrightarrow H^{\mathcal{Q}}
(cf.
Lemma

17
).
For
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models\mathcal{A}
:
Assume that
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\models\mathcal{A}
.
Then there is a word
a_{1}\dots a_{m}\in[\mathcal{A}]
such that
G(a_{1}\dots a_{m})\longrightarrow H^{\mathcal{Q}}
.
By
a_{1}\dots a_{m}\in[\mathcal{A}]
, there are
z_{0},\dots,z_{m}\in|\mathcal{A}|
such that

\langle z_{0},z_{m}\rangle=\langle\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}},\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\rangle
and for
k\in[m]
,
z_{k}\in\delta_{a_{k}}^{\mathcal{A}}(z_{k-1})
.
By
G(a_{1}\dots a_{m})\longrightarrow H^{\mathcal{Q}}
, there are
l_{0},\dots,l_{m}\in|H|
such that

\langle l_{0},l_{m}\rangle=\langle\mathsf{1}^{H},\mathsf{2}^{H}\rangle
and for
k\in[m]
,
\langle l_{k-1},l_{k}\rangle\in a_{k}^{H}
.
Then,

Sublemma
.

For every
k\in[0,m]
,
z_{k}\in U_{l_{k}}
.

Proof.

By induction on
k
.
Case
k=0
:
By
\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}}\in{U}_{\mathsf{1}^{H}}

(P-s-t)
.
Case
k\geq 1
:
We have

\displaystyle z_{k}\in\delta_{a_{k}}^{\mathcal{A}}(z_{k-1})

\displaystyle\subseteq\delta_{a_{k}}^{\mathcal{A}}({U}_{l_{k-1}})

(By
z_{k-1}\in{U}_{l_{k-1}}
(IH))

\displaystyle\subseteq{U}_{l_{k}}.

(By
\langle l_{k-1},l_{k}\rangle\in a_{k}^{H}

(P-Con’)
) ∎

Since
z_{m}\in{U}_{l_{m}}
contradicts
\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\not\in{U}_{\mathsf{2}^{H}}

(P-s-t)
,

H^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models\mathcal{A}
.

\Longrightarrow
:
We define
P=\langle G,\{U_{i}\}_{i\in|G|}\rangle
as follows:

•

G
is the edge extension of
G(w)
such that

a^{G}=a^{H}
for
a\in\{\mathsf{I},\overline{\mathsf{I}}\}
and
a^{G}=a^{G(w)}
for
a\in\Sigma^{(-)}
;

•

each set
U_{i}\subseteq|\mathcal{A}|
is defined by:

\displaystyle z\in U_{i}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\iff$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 5.0pt}}\exists v\in[{\mathcal{A}}[\_,z]].\ G(v)\longrightarrow{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[\_,[i]_{H}].

Here,
{\mathcal{A}}[\_,z]
denotes the graph
\mathcal{A}
in which
\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}
has been replaced with
z
(similarly for
H^{\mathcal{Q}}[\_,[i]_{H}]
).

Then
P
is a saturable path for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
, as follows.

Sublemma
.

Let
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
.
If
G(a)\longrightarrow{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[[i]_{H},[j]_{H}]
, then

\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
.
(Here,
{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[[i]_{H},[j]_{H}]
denotes the graph
{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}
in which
\mathsf{1}^{{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}}
and
\mathsf{2}^{{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}}
have been replaced with
[i]_{H}
and
[j]_{H}
, respectively.)

Proof.

Let
z\in U_{i}
.
By definition,
there is
v\in[\mathcal{A}[\_,z]]
such that
G(v)\longrightarrow{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[\_,[i]_{H}]
.
Combining with
G(a)\longrightarrow{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[[i]_{H},[j]_{H}]
yields
G(va)\longrightarrow{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[\_,[j]_{H}]
.
Thus, for every
z^{\prime}\in\delta_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(z)
,
z^{\prime}\in U_{j}
.
Hence
\delta_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i})\subseteq U_{j}
.
Similarly by
G(\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{277133}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{277133}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{227418}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{203012}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits})\longrightarrow{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[[j]_{H},[i]_{H}]
,
\delta_{\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{227418}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{227418}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{135795}{124882}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.63779pt$\hss\resizebox{96996}{89202}{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle a\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{j})\subseteq U_{i}
.
∎

For
(P-s-t)
:

\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}}\in U_{\mathsf{1}^{G}}
is shown by considering
v=\mathsf{I}
.

\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\not\in U_{\mathsf{2}^{G}}
is because
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models\mathcal{A}
.
For
(P-Con)
:
Let
\langle i,j\rangle\in a^{G}
.
Because
G(a)\longrightarrow{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[[i]_{H},[j]_{H}]
(since
H
is a saturation of
G
),
we have
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
(the sub-lemma).
For
(P-Sat)
:
For every
a\in\Sigma
and
i,j\in|G|
,
because either
G(a)\longrightarrow{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[[i]_{H},[j]_{H}]
or
G(\overline{a})\longrightarrow{H^{\mathcal{Q}}}[[i]_{H},[j]_{H}]
always holds,
we have
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})\lor\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{a}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
(the sub-lemma).
∎

Theorem 33
.

For two NFAs
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
, TFAE:

•

\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}
.

•

\exists w\in[\mathcal{A}].\
there is a saturable path for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{B}
.

Proof.

We have

\displaystyle\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}

\displaystyle\iff\exists w\in[\mathcal{A}].\exists H\in\mathcal{S}(G(w)).\ H^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}

(
Lemma

21
)

\displaystyle\iff\exists w\in[\mathcal{A}].\exists H\in\mathcal{S}(G(w)).\ H^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models w\leq\mathcal{B}

(Because
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\models w
and
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\models\mathcal{A}
by
H\in\mathcal{S}(G(w))
)

\displaystyle\iff\exists w\in[\mathcal{A}].\ \mbox{there is a saturable path for $\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{B}$}.

(
Lemma

32
) ∎

V-C

Exponential-size model property

The characterization by saturable paths (
Theorem

33
) gives another bounded model property for
ExKA
terms (cf.
Lemma

21
) as follows.
The following proof is an analogy of the well-known pumping lemma from automata theory.

Lemma 34

(Exponential-size model property)
.

For every NFAs
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
,
if
{}\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}
, then
there is a
2
-pointed structure
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}
of size
\#(|\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}|)\leq\#(|\mathcal{A}|)\times 2^{\#(|\mathcal{B}|)}

such that
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}
.

Proof.

By
Theorem

33
, there are a word
w=a_{1}\dots a_{n}\in[\mathcal{A}]
and a saturable path
P=\langle G,\{U_{i}\}_{i\in[0,n]}\rangle
for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{B}
.
Without loss of generality, we can assume that
n
is the minimum among such words.
Since
w\in[\mathcal{A}]
, let
\{s_{i}\}_{i\in[0,n]}
be such that

\langle s_{0},s_{n}\rangle=\langle\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}},\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\rangle
and
s_{x}\in\delta_{a_{i}}^{\mathcal{A}}(s_{i-1})
for
i\in[n]
.
Assume that
n+1>\#(|\mathcal{A}|)\times 2^{\#(|\mathcal{B}|)}
.
By the pigeonhole principle, there are
0\leq x<y\leq n
s.t.
\langle s_{x},U_{x}\rangle=\langle s_{y},U_{y}\rangle
.
Let
w^{\prime}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}a_{1}\dots a_{x}a_{y+1}\dots a_{n}
.
Let
P^{\prime}
be the
P
in which
the source of the edge for

Theorem 35
.

The equational theory of
ExKA
terms (w.r.t. binary relations) is decidable in coNEXP.

Proof.

Similarly for
lemma

22
,
it suffices to show that the following problem is in NEXP: given
ExKA
terms
t,s
, does
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s
hold?
By
Lemma

34
(with
Proposition

26
), we can give the following algorithm:

1.

Take a
2
-pointed structure
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}
of size
\#(|\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}|)\leq\#(|\mathcal{A}_{t}|)\times 2^{\#(|\mathcal{A}_{s}|)}
, non-deterministically.
Here,
\mathcal{A}_{t}
and
\mathcal{A}_{s}
are the NFAs obtained from
t
and
s
, respectively (
Definition

25
).

2.

Return
\mathsf{true}
, if
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\not\models t\leq s
;
\mathsf{false}
, otherwise.

Then
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s
, if some execution returns
\mathsf{true}
;
\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s
, otherwise.
Here,
\ddot{\mathfrak{A}}\not\models t\leq s
can be decided in exponential time (
Proposition

20
).
∎

V-D

From saturable paths to word automata

For some cases, for an NFA
\mathcal{A}
, we can construct an NFA
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}
such that:
for every word
w
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\}
, TFAE:

•

w\in[\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}]
;

•

there is a saturable path for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
.

To this end, first, let

\varphi(\mathcal{U},U)\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigwedge\begin{cases}U\times(|\mathcal{A}|\setminus U)\times U\times(|\mathcal{A}|\setminus U)\subseteq\mathcal{U}\\

\displaystyle\xi(U)

\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\forall\langle i,j\rangle\in[0,n]^{2}.\forall a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}.\forall\langle t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},t_{4}\rangle\in\nu(U_{i}).\ \xi(U_{j})

Definition 37
.

For an NFA
\mathcal{A}
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
, let
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}
be the NFA over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
defined by:

•

|\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}|\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{\blacktriangleright,\blacktriangleleft\}\cup\{\langle\mathcal{U},U\rangle\in\wp(|\mathcal{A}|^{4})\times\wp(|\mathcal{A}|)\mid\varphi(\mathcal{U},{U})\land\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}({U})\subseteq{U}\}

•

\mathsf{I}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
is the minimal set such that

–

for all

\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}}\in U

\langle\blacktriangleright,\langle\mathcal{U},U\rangle\rangle\in\mathsf{I}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}

–

for all

s.t.
\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\not\in U
,
\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}\rangle,\blacktriangleleft\rangle\in\mathsf{I}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
;

•

for each
a\in\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
,
a^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}

,

\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}\rangle,\langle\mathcal{U},{U}^{\prime}\rangle\rangle\in a^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
holds;

•

\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}={\blacktriangleright}
and
\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}={\blacktriangleleft}
.

\blacktriangleright

.

Using this transformation,
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}
satisfies the following:

Lemma 38

(Completeness (of
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}
))
.

For every NFA
\mathcal{A}
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
and word
w
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\}
,
we have:

w\in[\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}]

\Longleftarrow
there is a saturable path for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
.

Proof.

Let
w=a_{1}\dots a_{n}
and
P=\langle G,\{{U}_{i}\}_{i\in[0,n]}\rangle
be a saturable path for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
.
Let
\mathcal{U}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-2.7431pt\raisebox{4.66875pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Delta$}}\hskip-2.7431pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{i\in[0,n]}{U}_{i}\times(|\mathcal{A}|\setminus{U}_{i})\times{U}_{i}\times(|\mathcal{A}|\setminus{U}_{i})
.
Then we have

•

\langle{\blacktriangleright},\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{0}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
(by
(P-s-t)
);

•

for all
i\in[n]
,
\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{i-1}\rangle,\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{i}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{a_{i}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
(by
(P-Con)
);

•

\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{n}\rangle,{\blacktriangleleft}\rangle\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
(by
(P-s-t)
).

Here, for
i\in[0,n]
,
\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{i}\rangle\in|\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}|
holds, because

\varphi(\mathcal{U},U_{i})
holds by
(P-Sat)
with
Lemma

36

and
\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i})\subseteq U_{i}
holds by
(P-Con)
.
Hence,
w\in[\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}]
.
∎

Lemma 39

(Soundness for the
\mathsf{I}^{-}
-free fragment)
.

For every NFA
\mathcal{A}
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
and word
w
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\}
,
if
\mathcal{A}
does not contain
\mathsf{I}^{-}
, then we have:

w\in[\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}]

\Longrightarrow
there is a saturable path for
\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
.

Proof.

Let
w=a_{1}\dots a_{n}
.
By the form of
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}
, there are
\mathcal{U}
,
{U}_{0}
,
\dots
, and
{U}_{n}
such that

•

\langle{\blacktriangleright},\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{0}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
;

•

for every
i\in[n]
,
\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{i-1}\rangle,\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{i}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{a_{i}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
;

•

\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{n}\rangle,{\blacktriangleleft}\rangle\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
.

Let
H
be the
\mathsf{I}
-saturation of
G(w)
such that

\mathsf{I}^{H}
is the identity relation.

H
is consistent, because
G(w)
is consistent and
\mathsf{I}^{H}
is the identity relation.

H
is an edge-extension of
G(w)
, because

\mathsf{I}^{H}\supseteq\mathsf{I}^{G(w)}=\emptyset
and
\overline{\mathsf{I}}^{H}=|H|^{2}\setminus\mathsf{I}^{H}\supseteq\overline{\mathsf{I}}^{G(w)}
.
Hence
H
is indeed an
\mathsf{I}
-saturation of
G(w)
.

Then
P=\langle H,\{U_{i}\}_{i\in[0,n]}\rangle
is a saturable path for
{}\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
as follows.
For
(P-s-t)
: By the definition of
\mathsf{I}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
,
\mathsf{1}^{\mathcal{A}}\in U_{0}
and
\mathsf{2}^{\mathcal{A}}\not\in U_{n}
.
For
(P-Con)
for
a\in\Sigma^{(-)}
: By the definition of
a_{i}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
,

\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{a_{i}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i-1},U_{i})
.
(Note that the other edges do not exist.)
For
(P-Con)
for
a=\mathsf{I}
:
Because
\mathsf{I}^{H}
is the identity relation
and
U_{i}\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i})
for every
i\in[0,n]
(by the definition of
|\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}|
).
For
(P-Con)
for
a=\overline{\mathsf{I}}
:
Because
\overline{\mathsf{I}}
does not occur in
\mathcal{A}
,
\delta_{\overline{\mathsf{I}}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i})=\emptyset\subseteq U_{j}
always holds for every
i,j\in[0,n]
.
Hence
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{\mathsf{I}}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
.
For
(P-Sat)
: Because
\mathcal{U}
satisfies
\varphi(\mathcal{U},{U}_{i})
for every
i\in[0,n]
(by the definition of
|\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}|
), with
Lemma

36
.
∎

Theorem 40
.

For every NFAs
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}
, over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
,
if
\mathcal{B}
does not contain
\mathsf{I}^{-}
, then we have

\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}\quad\iff\quad[\mathcal{A}]\cap[\mathcal{B}^{\mathcal{S}}]\neq\emptyset.

Proof.

We have

\displaystyle\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}

\displaystyle\iff\exists w\in[\mathcal{A}].\ \mbox{there is a saturable path for $\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{B}$}.

(
Theorem

33
)

\displaystyle\iff\exists w\in[\mathcal{A}].\ w\in[\mathcal{B}^{\mathcal{S}}]

(
Lemmas

38
,
39
)

\displaystyle\iff[\mathcal{A}]\cap[\mathcal{B}^{\mathcal{S}}]\neq\emptyset.

∎

Theorem 41
.

The equational theory of
ExKA
terms without
\mathsf{I}^{-}
(w.r.t. binary relations) is PSPACE-complete.

Proof.

For hardness:
By
Proposition

4
, as the term class subsumes
\mathcal{T}_{\{\cdot,\cup,\_^{*}\}}
.
For upper bound:
Similar to
lemma

22
, with (co-)NPSPACE = PSPACE (Savitch’s theorem
[
33
]
), it suffices to show that the following problem is in NPSPACE:
given
ExKA
terms
t,s
without
\mathsf{I}^{-}
, does
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}t\leq s
hold?
By
Theorem

40
(with
Proposition

26
),
we can reduce this problem into the emptiness problem of NFAs (of size exponential in the input).
Therefore, by using a standard on-the-fly algorithm for the non-emptiness problem of NFAs (which is essentially the graph reachability problem),
we can give a non-deterministic polynomial space algorithm.
∎

V-E

Remark on the case of full
ExKA
terms

Additionally, we remark that the soundness also holds for
ExKA
terms without complements of term variables.

Lemma 42

(Soundness for the
a^{-}
-free fragment, cf.
Lemma

39
)
.

For every NFA
\mathcal{A}
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
and word
w
over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}\setminus\{\mathsf{I}\}
,
if
w
does not contain
a^{-}
for any
a\in\Sigma
, then we have:

w\in[\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}]

\Longrightarrow
there is a saturable path for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
.

Proof.

Let
w=a_{1}\dots a_{n}
.
By the form of
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}
, there are
\mathcal{U}
,
{U}_{0}
,
\dots
, and
{U}_{n}
such that

•

\langle{\blacktriangleright},\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{0}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
;

•

for every
i\in[n]
,
\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{i-1}\rangle,\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{i}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{a_{i}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
;

•

\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{n}\rangle,{\blacktriangleleft}\rangle\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
.

Let
H
be the
\mathsf{I}
-saturation of
G(w)
such that

\mathsf{I}^{H}=\{\langle i,j\rangle\in[0,n]^{2}\mid i=j\lor\lnot\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{\mathsf{I}}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})\}.

We have
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{\mathsf{I}}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})\lor\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
because
\mathcal{U}
satisfies
\varphi(\mathcal{U},{U}_{i})
for every
i\in[0,n]
(
Lemma

36
).
If
\lnot\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{\mathsf{I}}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
, then
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
; thus
U_{i}=U_{j}
.
Therefore, the binary relation
\{\langle i,j\rangle\in[0,n]^{2}\mid\lnot\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{\mathsf{I}}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})\}
is symmetric and transitive;
thus
\mathsf{I}^{H}
is an equivalence relation.
Additionally,
H
is consistent, because
a^{-}
does not occur in
H
for any
a\in\Sigma
.

H
is an edge-extension of
G(w)
, because

\mathsf{I}^{H}\supseteq\mathsf{I}^{G(w)}=\emptyset
and
\overline{\mathsf{I}}^{H}\supseteq\overline{\mathsf{I}}^{G(w)}
(by the definition of
\mathsf{I}^{H}
).
Hence
H
is indeed an
\mathsf{I}
-saturation of
G(w)
.

Then
P=\langle H,\{U_{i}\}_{i\in[0,n]}\rangle
is a saturable path for
{}\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
as follows.
For
(P-s-t)
,
(P-Sat)
, and
(P-Con)
for
a\in\Sigma^{(-)}
: Similarly for
Lemma

39
.
For
(P-Con)
for
a=\mathsf{I}
:
for every
\langle i,j\rangle\in\mathsf{I}^{H}
,
if
i=j
, then
\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i})\subseteq U_{j}
by the definition of
|\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}|
; thus
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
.
If
\lnot\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{\mathsf{I}}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
, then
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
by
(P-Sat)
.
For
(P-Con)
for
a=\overline{\mathsf{I}}
:
By the definition of
\mathsf{I}^{H}
,
we have
\mathop{\mathrm{Con}}\nolimits_{\overline{\mathsf{I}}}^{\mathcal{A}}(U_{i},U_{j})
for every
\langle i,j\rangle\in[0,n]^{2}\setminus\mathsf{I}^{H}
.
∎

Theorem 43
.

For every NFAs
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}
, over
\Sigma_{\mathsf{I}}^{(-,\smile)}
,
if
\mathcal{A}
does not contain
a^{-}
for any
a\in\Sigma
, then we have

\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{B}\quad\iff\quad[\mathcal{A}]\cap[\mathcal{B}^{\mathcal{S}}]\neq\emptyset.

Proof.

Cf.
Theorem

40
(use
Lemma

42
instead of
Lemma

39
).
∎

Theorem 44
.

The equational theory of
ExKA
terms without
a^{-}
for any
a\in\Sigma
(w.r.t. binary relations) is PSPACE-complete.

Proof.

Cf.
Theorem

41
(use
Theorem

43
instead of
Theorem

40
).
∎

However, we leave open the precise complexity of the equational theory of
ExKA
terms, while it is decidable in coNEXP (
Theorem

35
) and at least PSPACE-hard (
Proposition

4
).
The problematic case is when both
\mathsf{I}^{-}
and
a^{-}
occur.
Our automata construction cannot apply to the full case, as follows:

Remark 45

(Failure of the automata construction (
Definition

37
) for (full)
ExKA
terms)
.

Consider the soundness (
Lemmas

39
,
42
) for
ExKA
terms:
for a given word
w\in[\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}]
, construct a saturable path for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
.
The essence of the proofs in
Lemmas

39
,
42

is that an
\mathsf{I}
-saturation of
G(w)
always exists.
However, for (full)
ExKA
terms, the situation is changed.
For example, let
\mathcal{A}
be the NFA obtained from the term
a\overline{\mathsf{I}}\cup\overline{\mathsf{I}}\overline{a}
(cf.
Equation

2
) and
w=ab\overline{a}
:

Then
w\in[\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}]
holds because

•

\langle{\blacktriangleright},\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{0}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
;

•

\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{0}\rangle,\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{1}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{a}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
;

•

\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{1}\rangle,\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{2}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{b}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
;

•

\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{2}\rangle,\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{3}\rangle\rangle\in\delta_{\overline{a}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
;

•

\langle\langle\mathcal{U},{U}_{3}\rangle,{\blacktriangleleft}\rangle\in\delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}}
,

by letting
U_{0}=U_{2}=\{\mathtt{A},\mathtt{D}\}
,
U_{1}=U_{3}=\{\mathtt{B},\mathtt{C}\}
,
and
\mathcal{U}=\bigcup_{i\in[0,3]}{U}_{i}\times(|\mathcal{A}|\setminus{U}_{i})\times{U}_{i}\times(|\mathcal{A}|\setminus{U}_{i})
.
However, there does not exist any saturable path for
\not\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
, because
{}\models_{\mathrm{REL}}w\leq\mathcal{A}
(
Equation

2
).
Additionally, if exists, an
\mathsf{I}
-saturation
H
of
G(w)
should satisfy
\langle 0,2\rangle\in\mathsf{I}^{H}
(by
\overline{\mathsf{I}}\overline{a}\in[\mathcal{A}]
) and
\langle 1,3\rangle\in\mathsf{I}^{H}
(by
a\overline{\mathsf{I}}\in[\mathcal{A}]
) for
H^{\mathcal{Q}}\not\models\mathcal{A}
:

Remark 46
.

One may think that
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}
behaves as a complement of an NFA
\mathcal{A}
(cf.
Theorems

43
,
40
).
Note that
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}
is not the language complement of an NFA
\mathcal{A}
, i.e., the following does not hold:
for every word
w
,
w\in[\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}}]\iff w\not\in[\mathcal{A}]
.
E.g., let
\mathcal{A}
be the NFA obtained from the term
a\cup\overline{a}
and
w=\mathsf{I}
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
